symptoms.name: Joint swelling
symptoms.description: Joint swelling is enlargement of a joint from synovial fluid (effusion), synovial thickening or swelling of the surrounding soft tissues. It distinguishes true arthritis from arthralgia alone and is characterized by the number and pattern of joints involved, acuity and the presence of warmth or redness.
symptoms.weight_rationale: Objective swelling separates inflammatory arthritis from simple joint pain and, combined with acuity and joint pattern, narrows the differential to arthritides, crystal disease, septic arthritis and viral arthritis such as chikungunya.
red_flags: Hot, red, swollen single joint with fever (possible septic arthritis)
Inability to bear weight or move the joint
Swelling after significant trauma
Rapidly spreading redness over the joint
Joint swelling in an immunocompromised patient

symptoms.name: Right upper abdominal pain (right upper quadrant)
symptoms.description: Right upper quadrant pain is pain localized beneath the right costal margin, overlying the liver, gallbladder and biliary tree, with contributions from the duodenum, right kidney, hepatic flexure and right lung base. Biliary pain is often steady and may radiate to the right scapula, whereas hepatic pain from capsular stretch is usually a dull ache accompanying hepatitis or congestion.
symptoms.weight_rationale: Localization to the right upper quadrant focuses the differential on hepatobiliary disease (cholecystitis, biliary colic, cholangitis, hepatitis), although duodenal, pancreatic, renal and basal pulmonary causes remain possible.
causes: Acute viral hepatitis (hepatitis A, hepatitis B)
Hepatic congestion in right heart failure
red_flags: Fever with jaundice and right upper quadrant pain (possible cholangitis)
Jaundice with confusion or bleeding tendency (possible acute liver failure)
Rigid abdomen or rebound tenderness
Hypotension or rapid heart rate
Persistent vomiting preventing oral intake

symptoms.name: Pale or clay-colored stools
symptoms.description: Pale, clay-colored (acholic) stools result from reduced delivery of bile pigments to the intestine, so that stercobilin no longer gives stool its normal brown color. The finding indicates cholestasis, either intrahepatic (hepatitis, cirrhosis) or extrahepatic (bile duct obstruction), and usually accompanies jaundice and dark urine.
symptoms.weight_rationale: Acholic stool points specifically to impaired bile flow and narrows the differential to hepatitis and biliary obstruction; with jaundice and dark urine it forms a characteristic cholestatic triad.
causes: Acute viral hepatitis (hepatitis A, hepatitis B)
Gallstones in the common bile duct
red_flags: Painless jaundice with weight loss (possible pancreatic or biliary malignancy)
Fever, rigors and right upper quadrant pain (possible cholangitis)
Confusion, drowsiness or bleeding (possible acute liver failure)
Pale stools persisting in an infant

symptoms.name: Itching (pruritus)
symptoms.description: Pruritus is an unpleasant skin sensation that provokes the desire to scratch. It may be localized, usually from primary skin disease, or generalized, when systemic causes such as cholestatic liver disease, chronic kidney disease, drug reactions or hematologic disorders are considered.
symptoms.weight_rationale: Itching is very common and nonspecific; it narrows the differential mainly when generalized without rash (suggesting systemic causes such as cholestasis) or when paired with a characteristic eruption such as varicella.
causes: Cholestatic liver disease (including cholestatic hepatitis A)
red_flags: Itching with hives, lip or tongue swelling or breathing difficulty (possible anaphylaxis)
Generalized itching with jaundice
Itching with unexplained weight loss, fever or night sweats
Widespread blistering or skin peeling

symptoms.name: Profuse watery ("rice-water") diarrhea
symptoms.description: Profuse watery diarrhea consists of large-volume, liquid stools; in cholera it is classically pale, flecked with mucus and described as "rice-water". Toxin-mediated intestinal secretion can cause losses of up to about a liter per hour in adults, producing severe dehydration and hypovolemic shock within hours if fluid is not replaced.
symptoms.weight_rationale: Painless, high-volume rice-water stools are highly characteristic of cholera and, in the right epidemiologic setting, strongly direct the diagnosis and urgent rehydration.
red_flags: Sunken eyes, very dry mouth or loss of skin turgor
Lethargy or unconsciousness
Weak or absent pulse or low blood pressure
Little or no urine output
Inability to drink or persistent vomiting
Muscle cramps with weakness (electrolyte loss)

symptoms.name: Signs of dehydration (sunken eyes, dry mouth, intense thirst)
symptoms.description: Dehydration is a deficit of body water and electrolytes from fluid losses exceeding intake, most often from diarrhea, vomiting, fever, sweating or osmotic diuresis. Clinical signs progress from thirst, dry mucous membranes and reduced dark urine to sunken eyes, reduced skin turgor, tachycardia, confusion and hypovolemic shock.
symptoms.weight_rationale: Dehydration reflects severity of fluid loss rather than a specific diagnosis; it narrows attention to diarrheal and vomiting illnesses, uncontrolled hyperglycemia and heat illness, and determines urgency of rehydration.
causes: Cholera and other acute infectious gastroenteritis
red_flags: Confusion, lethargy or loss of consciousness
Seizures
No urine output or very dark amber urine
Rapid heartbeat or low blood pressure
Inability to keep fluids down

symptoms.name: Muscle cramps
symptoms.description: Muscle cramps are sudden, involuntary and painful contractions of a muscle or muscle group, commonly the calves and feet. They occur with overuse and dehydration and with electrolyte disturbances such as hypokalemia, hyponatremia and hypocalcemia, as in the large fluid and electrolyte losses of cholera.
symptoms.weight_rationale: Cramps are common and mostly benign; they gain significance mainly alongside profuse diarrhea, diuretic use or renal disease, where they suggest electrolyte depletion.
causes: Electrolyte depletion (low sodium, potassium or calcium), including in cholera
red_flags: Cramps with profuse watery diarrhea and weakness
Cramps with muscle weakness or palpitations (possible severe electrolyte disturbance)
Severe, persistent cramps not relieved by stretching
Cramps with dark urine after exertion

symptoms.name: Pain or tingling at an animal-bite site
symptoms.description: Pain, itching, tingling or burning at a healed or healing animal-bite or scratch wound can mark the prodrome of rabies as the virus reaches the dorsal root ganglia. It typically appears with nonspecific fever, malaise and headache weeks to months after the exposure and precedes the neurologic phase.
symptoms.weight_rationale: New paresthesia at a prior animal-bite site in a febrile patient is a classic early clue to rabies, which is nearly always fatal once clinical signs appear.
red_flags: Fever, headache or malaise after a dog, cat or bat exposure
Fear of water or throat spasms on swallowing
Agitation, confusion or hallucinations
Weakness or paralysis starting in the bitten limb
Incomplete or absent post-exposure prophylaxis after the bite

symptoms.name: Fear of water / throat spasms on swallowing (hydrophobia)
symptoms.description: Hydrophobia is a terrifying, involuntary spasm of the pharyngeal, laryngeal and inspiratory muscles provoked by attempts to drink, and in time by the sight, sound or even thought of water. It is the hallmark of furious (encephalitic) rabies and is often accompanied by aerophobia, spasms triggered by a draft of air on the face.
symptoms.weight_rationale: Hydrophobia is essentially pathognomonic of rabies encephalitis, especially with a history of animal bite, and signals a disease that is fatal once symptomatic.
red_flags: History of a dog, cat or bat bite or scratch
Agitation, hallucinations or fluctuating consciousness
Excessive salivation or drooling
Aerophobia (spasms with air on the face)
Progressive paralysis or coma

symptoms.name: Excessive salivation / drooling
symptoms.description: Hypersalivation and drooling result from excess saliva production or, more often, from an inability to retain or swallow normal saliva. Causes range from oral and pharyngeal infections to neurologic disorders that impair swallowing, and in rabies drooling reflects both autonomic stimulation and painful pharyngeal spasms.
symptoms.weight_rationale: Drooling has a broad differential (oral infection, neuromuscular disease, medications); it gains weight when combined with hydrophobia and agitation after an animal bite, as in rabies.
causes: Painful mouth ulcers (e.g., hand, foot and mouth disease)
Stroke, Parkinson disease or ALS (impaired swallowing)
red_flags: Drooling with difficulty breathing or noisy breathing
Drooling with inability to swallow and fever (possible epiglottitis or deep neck abscess)
Drooling with fear of water or agitation after an animal bite
Sudden drooling with facial droop or slurred speech

symptoms.name: Agitation, anxiety or hallucinations
symptoms.description: Agitation is a state of excessive motor and mental restlessness with irritability or anxiety, which may be accompanied by hallucinations when perception is disturbed. It arises from psychiatric illness but also from delirium due to infection, metabolic disturbance, intoxication or withdrawal, and is a feature of furious rabies.
symptoms.weight_rationale: Agitation is nonspecific, but new agitation or hallucinations with fever suggest delirium or encephalitis (including rabies) and mandate urgent evaluation.
causes: Delirium from systemic infection, hypoxia or metabolic disturbance
red_flags: Fever with agitation or hallucinations (possible encephalitis or sepsis)
Recent animal bite with fear of water or drooling
Threats of self-harm or harm to others
Seizures or reduced level of consciousness
Low oxygen saturation or low blood glucose

symptoms.name: Abdominal swelling (distension or ascites)
symptoms.description: Abdominal swelling is enlargement of the abdomen from gas, fluid, organ enlargement or masses. Ascites, free fluid in the peritoneal cavity, most often results from portal hypertension and low serum albumin in chronic liver disease, including the periportal fibrosis of chronic Schistosoma japonicum infection, and is suggested by shifting dullness and a fluid wave.
symptoms.weight_rationale: Distension alone is nonspecific (gas, obesity, pregnancy); demonstrable ascites narrows the differential to cirrhosis and portal hypertension, heart failure, malignancy and hypoalbuminemic states.
causes: Cirrhosis and portal hypertension (e.g., chronic hepatitis B, alcohol)
Gas and bloating, irritable bowel syndrome
red_flags: Fever and abdominal pain with ascites (possible spontaneous bacterial peritonitis)
Vomiting blood or black stools (possible variceal bleeding)
Confusion or jaundice
Distension with vomiting and no passage of stool or gas (possible obstruction)
Breathing difficulty from tense ascites

symptoms.name: Blood in stool (hematochezia)
symptoms.description: Hematochezia is the passage of bright red or maroon blood per rectum, alone or mixed with stool. It usually indicates a colonic, rectal or anal source, although brisk upper gastrointestinal bleeding can also present this way; bloody diarrhea with fever suggests invasive infectious or inflammatory colitis.
symptoms.weight_rationale: Visible blood localizes the problem to the gastrointestinal tract, most often the lower tract, but the range of causes remains wide from hemorrhoids to colitis, schistosomiasis and colorectal cancer.
red_flags: Dizziness, fainting or low blood pressure
Large volume or ongoing bleeding
Rapid heart rate
Severe abdominal pain
Unexplained weight loss or change in bowel habit (possible malignancy)
Anticoagulant or antiplatelet use

symptoms.name: Coughing fits with a "whoop" (paroxysmal cough)
symptoms.description: Paroxysmal cough consists of bursts of rapid, uncontrollable coughs on a single expiration, followed by a forced inspiration against a partially closed glottis that produces the characteristic high-pitched whoop. It is the defining feature of the paroxysmal stage of pertussis, although the whoop is often absent in young infants and in adolescents and adults.
symptoms.weight_rationale: Paroxysms with an inspiratory whoop are highly characteristic of pertussis and strongly narrow the differential, though absence of the whoop does not exclude it.
causes: Adenovirus and other respiratory viral infections
red_flags: Apnea or pauses in breathing, especially in infants
Cyanosis during or after coughing
Seizures
Inability to feed or signs of dehydration
Young infant, unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated

symptoms.name: Vomiting after coughing fits (post-tussive vomiting)
symptoms.description: Post-tussive vomiting is vomiting provoked by a severe bout of coughing, caused by the rise in intrathoracic and intra-abdominal pressure and vagal stimulation during paroxysms. It is a characteristic feature of pertussis and should prompt consideration of that diagnosis whenever vomiting follows coughing.
symptoms.weight_rationale: Vomiting triggered by coughing paroxysms is a recognized clinical criterion for pertussis and considerably raises its likelihood, although forceful coughing from other causes can occasionally do the same.
red_flags: Signs of dehydration or poor feeding
Apnea or cyanosis with coughing spells
Weight loss in an infant
Blood in the vomitus

symptoms.name: Painful mouth sores or ulcers
symptoms.description: Mouth sores are painful breaks or vesicles in the oral mucosa that often cause difficulty eating, drinking and swallowing. Most are aphthous, traumatic or viral (herpes simplex, enteroviruses in hand, foot and mouth disease), but persistent ulcers may reflect systemic, autoimmune, immunodeficient or malignant disease.
symptoms.weight_rationale: Oral ulcers are common and usually benign; they narrow the differential when combined with a pattern such as a hand-foot rash in a child (HFMD) or vesicles elsewhere (varicella).
causes: Hand, foot and mouth disease (enterovirus, coxsackievirus)
Trauma from teeth, dentures or hot food
red_flags: Refusal to drink or signs of dehydration (especially in children)
Lethargy, seizures, persistent vomiting or breathing difficulty in a child with HFMD (possible neurologic complication)
Sores lasting more than two weeks
Sores with widespread rash or skin peeling after a new medicine
Sores in an immunocompromised patient

symptoms.name: Blister-like rash (vesicles)
symptoms.description: A vesicular rash consists of small (under about 1 cm), fluid-filled elevations of the skin. In varicella the vesicles appear in successive crops, starting on the face and trunk, so lesions at all stages from macules to crusts coexist; other patterns include grouped vesicles (herpes simplex), dermatomal vesicles (zoster) and hand-foot-mouth distributions (enterovirus).
symptoms.weight_rationale: Vesicles narrow the differential to a limited group of viral, contact and bullous conditions, and the pattern (crops at different stages, dermatomal, hand-foot-mouth) often points to a specific diagnosis.
red_flags: Rash with cough and breathing difficulty (possible varicella pneumonia)
Confusion, unsteady gait or severe headache (possible encephalitis or cerebellar ataxia)
Spreading redness, warmth or pus around lesions (secondary bacterial infection)
Hemorrhagic lesions or rash in an immunocompromised patient
Chickenpox in pregnancy or in a newborn
Widespread blistering with mucosal involvement

symptoms.name: Swollen lymph nodes (lymphadenopathy)
symptoms.description: Lymphadenopathy is enlargement of lymph nodes in size, consistency or number, localized to one region or generalized across two or more non-contiguous regions. Most is reactive to infection, but size, consistency, fixation, location (especially supraclavicular) and duration help separate benign from malignant or systemic causes.
symptoms.weight_rationale: Enlarged nodes are common and mostly reactive; generalized lymphadenopathy or hard, fixed or supraclavicular nodes narrow the differential toward HIV, tuberculosis, lymphoma and metastatic cancer.
causes: Local bacterial or viral infections (pharyngitis, dental and skin infections)
red_flags: Hard, fixed or matted nodes
Supraclavicular node enlargement
Nodes enlarging or persisting beyond several weeks
Fever, night sweats and unexplained weight loss
Generalized lymphadenopathy

symptoms.name: White patches in the mouth (oral thrush)
symptoms.description: Oral thrush is Candida overgrowth in the mouth, classically forming creamy white, curd-like plaques on the tongue, buccal mucosa and palate that can be wiped off to leave a red, sometimes bleeding surface. Outside infancy, denture use, antibiotics and inhaled or systemic corticosteroids, it suggests impaired cell-mediated immunity and is an important clinical marker of HIV infection.
symptoms.weight_rationale: Wipeable white plaques are highly characteristic of candidiasis, and unexplained thrush in an adult strongly suggests immunosuppression, notably HIV, or uncontrolled diabetes.
red_flags: Pain or difficulty swallowing (possible esophageal candidiasis)
Thrush in an adult without an obvious cause (possible undiagnosed HIV)
Unexplained weight loss, fever or chronic diarrhea
Thrush in a patient on chemotherapy or immunosuppressants
